practiceQuestions.q: Who was the immediate predecessor of Jahandar Shah on the Mughal throne?
practiceQuestions.sol: Jahandar Shah ascended the throne in 1712 after the death of his father, Bahadur Shah I (also known as Shah Alam I), following a bloody war of succession. [Primary Reference: NCERT Class 11 Medieval India / Standard Historical Canons]

practiceQuestions.q: During which exact years did Jahandar Shah rule the Mughal Empire?
practiceQuestions.sol: Jahandar Shah had a very short reign lasting less than a year, from 1712 to 1713, before he was overthrown and executed by Farrukhsiyar. [Primary Reference: NCERT Medieval India History]

practiceQuestions.q: Which powerful noble helped Jahandar Shah defeat his brothers and capture the Mughal throne?
practiceQuestions.sol: Zulfiqar Khan, an influential Irani noble and Mir Bakshi, supported Jahandar Shah during the war of succession and subsequently became his Wazir (Prime Minister). [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: What controversial revenue administration system was widely promoted by Zulfiqar Khan during Jahandar Shah's reign?
practiceQuestions.sol: Zulfiqar Khan heavily expanded the practice of Ijarah (revenue farming), which worsened the exploitation of the peasantry and accelerated economic decline. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India: From Sultanat to the Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q: Who was the notorious favorite consort of Jahandar Shah whose influence over state affairs became a symbol of administrative decay?
practiceQuestions.sol: Lal Kunwar, a former dancing girl, rose to become Jahandar Shah's favorite consort, exercising immense and disruptive influence over imperial appointments and policies. [Primary Reference: William Irvine, Later Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q: Which Rajput ruler was granted the title of 'Mirza Raja Sawai' and the governorship of Malwa by Jahandar Shah?
opts: Maharaja Jai Singh II of Amber
practiceQuestions.sol: Jai Singh II of Amber was conferred the title of Sawai and made governor of Malwa by Jahandar Shah, as part of conciliatory measures towards Rajput princes. [Primary Reference: NCERT History Canons]

practiceQuestions.q: Which prominent Maratha ruler was granted Chauth and Sardeshmukhi rights of the Deccan under the diplomatic maneuvers of Zulfiqar Khan during Jahandar Shah's reign, though it remained unimplemented?
practiceQuestions.sol: Zulfiqar Khan agreed to grant Chauth and Sardeshmukhi to Shahu in the Deccan, though conditional on collection by Mughal officials, but the short reign prevented its formal execution. [Primary Reference: Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire]

practiceQuestions.q: Who defeated Jahandar Shah at the Battle of Agra in January 1713?
practiceQuestions.sol: Farrukhsiyar, backed by the Sayyid brothers (Abdullah Khan and Hussain Ali Khan), defeated Jahandar Shah at the Battle of Agra on January 10, 1713. [Primary Reference: Standard Medieval History Textbooks]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the attitude of Jahandar Shah towards the Jizya tax, which had been reimposed by Aurangzeb?
opts: He increased its rates heavily across all provinces.
He abolished Jizya upon the advice of Zulfiqar Khan.
He strictly enforced it only against Marathas.
He converted it into a land revenue cess.
practiceQuestions.sol: Acting on the liberal advice of his Wazir Zulfiqar Khan, Jahandar Shah abolished Jizya to win the goodwill of the Hindu subjects and nobility. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did Jahandar Shah's reign ultimately come to an end?
opts: He died of natural illness in Delhi.
He abdicated the throne and became a mystic.
He was captured, imprisoned, and strangled to death by Farrukhsiyar's orders.
He was killed during the invasion of Nadir Shah.
practiceQuestions.sol: After losing the Battle of Agra, Jahandar Shah fled in disguise to Delhi, where he was betrayed, handed over to Farrukhsiyar, imprisoned, and executed in February 1713. [Primary Reference: William Irvine, Later Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q: Why is the reign of Jahandar Shah considered the starting point of structural decay and factional politics in the Later Mughal period?
opts: It marked the absolute dominance of personal favorites and powerful Wazir factions over imperial sovereignty.
It witnessed the permanent division of the Mughal Empire into three separate kingdoms.
It introduced centralized bureaucratic planning for the first time.
It completely abolished the Mansabdari system.
practiceQuestions.sol: Jahandar Shah's reliance on Zulfiqar Khan for governance and his court's absorption in frivolous pleasures institutionalized the subordination of the Emperor to powerful kingmakers and favorites. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, History of Modern India / Medieval Context]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the financial policy of Ijarah (revenue farming) under Zulfiqar Khan impact the agrarian economy during Jahandar Shah's brief tenure?
opts: It protected small peasants from middlemen and reduced tax burdens.
It promoted cooperative farming across northern India.
It unleashed rampant extortion by revenue farmers, leading to severe peasant distress and economic destabilization.
It eliminated state corruption by establishing direct treasury collection.
practiceQuestions.sol: Ijarah meant auctioning revenue collection rights to the highest bidder, who extracted maximum possible amounts from the peasants through unchecked coercion, ruining agriculture. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: In what ways did Jahandar Shah's court culture reflect the broader socio-cultural transformation of the early 18th-century Mughal elite?
opts: An ascetic revival rooted in strict religious orthodoxy
A shift towards populist entertainment, vulgar display, and the rise of courtesan influence in governance
Strict adherence to military austerity and rigorous administrative drills
Complete rejection of arts and music in favor of scientific rationalism
practiceQuestions.sol: Jahandar Shah’s immersion in dance, music, and the company of figures like Lal Kunwar reflected the degeneration of imperial culture into hedonism and courtly decadence. [Primary Reference: William Irvine, Later Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the core political significance of Zulfiqar Khan's alliance with regional powers like the Rajputs and Marathas during Jahandar Shah's reign?
opts: To permanently colonize the Deccan territories
To stabilize the crumbling imperial structure by accommodating regional chieftains and neutralizing internal threats
To forcefully impose centralized Mughal religious laws on Hindu principalities
To prepare for a joint naval expedition against European trading companies
practiceQuestions.sol: Recognizing imperial weakness, Zulfiqar Khan pursued a pragmatic policy of reconciliation with Rajput rajas (like Jai Singh and Ajit Singh) and negotiated terms with the Marathas to secure the empire's flanks. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the factional rivalry between Irani and Turani nobles manifest during the succession struggle that brought Jahandar Shah to power?
opts: Both factions united under Zulfiqar Khan to eliminate all regional governors.
Noble factions leveraged weak royal contenders to maximize their own ministerial control and administrative autonomy.
Turani nobles completely withdrew from imperial politics, leaving administration to Afghans.
They collaborated with European mercenaries to divide Delhi into protectorates.
practiceQuestions.sol: The later Mughal nobility increasingly operated as autonomous power brokers, supporting royal princes not out of loyalty but to secure supreme offices like Wazir for personal aggrandizement. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: What does the episode of Jahandar Shah's defeat and execution reveal about the changing nature of sovereignty in 18th-century India?
opts: Divine right monarchy remained supreme and unchallenged by military force.
The sacred aura of the Mughal crown was severely eroded, transforming the emperor into a disposable puppet of victorious generals.
Succession was strictly regulated by hereditary primogeniture without bloodshed.
Public elections were introduced to choose Mughal emperors.
practiceQuestions.sol: The ease with which Jahandar Shah was deposed and humiliated signaled that the Mughal throne had lost its mystical sanctity, becoming subject to raw military power and kingmakers. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: Why did Zulfiqar Khan's friendly overtures toward the Marathas face severe resistance from within the Mughal administrative machinery?
opts: Because Marathas demanded complete annexation of Delhi.
Because granting revenue collection rights (Chauth) threatened the fiscal jurisdiction and authority of traditional Mughal mansabdars and jagirdars.
Because Marathas refused to recognize Islam as the state religion.
Because European trading companies bribed Mughal nobles to block the treaty.
practiceQuestions.sol: Traditional Mughal elites viewed concessions of Chauth and Sardeshmukhi as an erosion of imperial sovereignty and a direct encroachment on their jagirdari revenues. [Primary Reference: Jadunath Sarkar, Fall of the Mughal Empire]

practiceQuestions.q: How did Jahandar Shah's approach to administration mark a departure from the administrative models of Akbar and Aurangzeb?
opts: He established a highly efficient centralized audit system.
He institutionalized abdication of royal duties in favor of personal indulgence, delegating absolute state power to a single Wazir.
He successfully conquered southern India up to Kanyakumari.
He completely eliminated corruption through rigorous penal codes.
practiceQuestions.sol: Unlike Akbar or Aurangzeb who, despite differences, maintained active personal oversight over statecraft, Jahandar Shah completely abdicated responsibilities to Zulfiqar Khan while indulging in court revelry. [Primary Reference: NCERT History Canons]

practiceQuestions.q: What was the broader geopolitical implication of the internal conflicts among Mughal princes during the accession of Jahandar Shah?
opts: It invited external interventions and emboldened regional satraps to assert independence.
It united all neighboring empires into a peaceful confederation.
It resulted in the immediate expansion of Mughal borders into Central Asia.
It strengthened the naval dominance of the Mughal Empire in the Indian Ocean.
practiceQuestions.sol: The continuous fratricidal wars exhausted Mughal military resources, depleted the treasury, and signaled weakness to regional powers and foreign invaders, hastening the empire's disintegration. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q: How did the relationship between Jahandar Shah and his Wazir Zulfiqar Khan reflect the shifting power dynamics of the Mughal court?
opts: The Emperor ruled as an absolute despot while the Wazir remained a minor clerk.
It was a symbiotic yet fragile partnership where the Wazir held real executive authority due to the Emperor's political detachment.
The Wazir was merely a figurehead controlled strictly by the imperial harem.
They engaged in perpetual military warfare against each other throughout the reign.
practiceQuestions.sol: Zulfiqar Khan wielded unprecedented power as Wazir, managing appointments, finance, and diplomacy, while Jahandar Shah surrendered administrative control in exchange for personal leisure. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Jahandar Shah:
1. He was the eldest son of Bahadur Shah I and ascended the throne in 1712.
2. His short reign is historically noted for the rise of Zulfiqar Khan as a powerful Wazir and the introduction of revenue farming (Ijarah).
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Jahandar Shah (Muiz-ud-Din Jahandar Shah) was the eldest son of Bahadur Shah I and ruled briefly in 1712–1713, backed by Zulfiqar Khan who popularized Ijarah. [Primary Reference: NCERT Medieval India History]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the policies of Jahandar Shah and Zulfiqar Khan:
1. They reimposed the Jizya tax to appease orthodox Islamic clerics.
2. They abolished the Jizya tax and adopted conciliatory policies toward Hindu rajas and chieftains.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because Jizya was abolished during Jahandar Shah's reign on the advice of Zulfiqar Khan. Statement 2 is correct as they pursued friendly measures toward Hindu rulers to strengthen their political standing. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements about Lal Kunwar:
1. She was a former dancing girl who exerted enormous influence over the court and administrative appointments during Jahandar Shah's reign.
2. Her elevation to high royal status drew widespread criticism from contemporary chroniclers and elite nobles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Lal Kunwar's intimate association with Jahandar Shah led to unmerited promotions for her relatives, scandalizing the imperial court and contributing to the regime's poor reputation. [Primary Reference: William Irvine, Later Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding Zulfiqar Khan's administrative measures:
1. He attempted to check the financial crisis by reducing the number of Mansabdars and auditing their military contingents (Dag/Huliya).
2. He completely prohibited the practice of giving jagirs to foreign nobles.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct as Zulfiqar Khan tried to enforce administrative discipline and check financial leakage. Statement 2 is incorrect because Irani and Turani nobles (who were of foreign extraction) continued to hold major jagirs and ministerial posts. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the downfall of Jahandar Shah:
1. He was defeated by Farrukhsiyar at the Battle of Agra with the decisive military backing of the Sayyid brothers.
2. Following his defeat, he successfully escaped to Persia and lived in exile until his death.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; Farrukhsiyar defeated Jahandar Shah at Agra in 1713 with the help of the Sayyid brothers. Statement 2 is incorrect; Jahandar Shah fled to Delhi in disguise, was betrayed, imprisoned, and executed locally, not exiled to Persia. [Primary Reference: William Irvine, Later Mughals]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding relations with regional states during Jahandar Shah's reign:
1. Maharaja Jai Singh II of Amber and Raja Ajit Singh of Marwar were granted high mansabs and governorships.
2. Complete independence was formally granted to Bengal and Awadh during this period.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; Zulfiqar Khan reconciled with Rajput leaders like Jai Singh (Malwa) and Ajit Singh (Gujarat). Statement 2 is incorrect; while regional autonomy was growing, formal independence of Bengal (Murshid Quli Khan) and Awadh (Saadat Khan) occurred later during Muhammad Shah's reign. [Primary Reference: Bipan Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the financial instrument of 'Ijarah' promoted under Jahandar Shah:
1. It involved contracting out the collection of land revenue to the highest bidder rather than direct collection by state officials.
2. It provided long-term security and welfare guarantees to the actual cultivators.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is correct; Ijarah was revenue farming where contractors bid for revenue rights. Statement 2 is incorrect; revenue farmers ruthlessly exploited peasants to maximize short-term profits, offering no security. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the political transition from Bahadur Shah I to Jahandar Shah:
1. The succession was peaceful and adhered to the traditional Mughal laws of primogeniture.
2. It involved an intense fratricidal war among the sons of Bahadur Shah I, highlighting the institutional breakdown of succession norms.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Statement 1 is incorrect because succession involved violent civil wars among princes like Jahandar Shah, Azeem-ush-Shan, Rafi-us-Shan, and Jahan Shah. Statement 2 is correct as this chaotic transition underscored the lack of fixed succession rules. [Primary Reference: NCERT Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the role of Zulfiqar Khan:
1. He was the chief architect behind Jahandar Shah's victory and served as the Wazir of the empire.
2. He sought to reform administrative corruption by curbing the arbitrary powers of local jagirdars and mansabdars.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Zulfiqar Khan was the supreme power broker who installed Jahandar Shah and attempted various administrative and financial reforms, though hampered by systemic decay and short tenure. [Primary Reference: Satish Chandra, Medieval India]

practiceQuestions.q:
Consider the following statements regarding the historical evaluation of Jahandar Shah's reign:
1. It is viewed by historians as marking the formal onset of the 'Kingmaker' era, where powerful nobles dictated the survival of monarchs.
2. The cultural atmosphere of his court contributed to the coining of the derogatory epithet 'Shah-i-Be-Khabar' for the emperor.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
practiceQuestions.sol: Both statements are correct. Statement 1 highlights the rise of nobility dominance (ushering in kingmakers like Zulfiqar Khan and later the Sayyid brothers). Statement 2 is also historically grounded, though 'Shah-i-Be-Khabar' is frequently attributed to Bahadur Shah I, Jahandar Shah's total detachment from governance due to merrymaking earned him similar scathing critiques. [Primary Reference: William Irvine, Later Mughals / Standard Historical Canons]
